items.html:
All of Botswana was covered by a white Google car without an antenna.

NOTE: Within Africa, this car can also be found in South Africa, Lesotho and Eswatini.

Botswana has white front plates and yellow rear plates, similar to UK-style plates.

NOTE: Botswana and Namibia are the only countries in southern Africa where yellow rear plates are predominantly found.

Signs in Botswana are usually in English. Most town names, however, are derived from any of the indigenous languages spoken in the country.

NOTE: The Afrikaans language, which is closely related to Dutch and common in South Africa, is very rare in Botswana. You will almost never find Afrikaans place names.

The typical Botswana landscape is dry and mostly flat, though a limited amount of elevation can be found in certain regions. Common vegetation includes shrubs, small trees, and occasionally dry, golden grasslands. The soil is arid, sandy and ranges in colour from white to red.

NOTE: The border region of South Africa can have a similar landscape.

Like the other countries in Southern Africa, outside road lines (if present) are yellow, while centre road lines are white.

NOTE: Outside yellow road lines in arid environments also exist in Israel, Palestine, Jordan, and the UAE. However, these countries all drive on the right side.

Botswana has a unique black-and-yellow striped signpost. More rarely, you can see red-and-white signposts.

NOTE: In Southern Africa, these signposts are only found in Botswana.
Curbs and guardrails are usually striped. Possible colour schemes are black-and-yellow, red-and-white, and black-and-white.

These small red-and-white chevrons can sometimes be found next to the road.

NOTE: They are also very common in South Africa.

Just like the other Southern African countries, direction signs have a green background.

The numbers of major roads start with A. These road numbers frequently appear on direction signs.

NOTE: Road numbers in South Africa never start with A.

Some road signs have a blue background. This is an older style of sign that was used before signs with white backgrounds were introduced. They are relatively unique to Botswana.

Note that most road signs will have the newer white background.

Typical Botswana houses range from small impoverished shacks to comfortable middle-class bungalows. Some buildings have exposed grey bricks. On occasion, you might find traditional round huts.

NOTE: All of these house styles are also found in the other southern African countries.

Random small blurs are common in Botswana’s coverage. These blurs are similar to the ones found on licence plates and faces, but they cover seemingly random parts of the panorama instead. This is especially noticeable in urban areas, and mostly absent on more rural roads.

Botswana has many unique and distinct regions throughout the country. This image breaks down the main factors that differentiate each distinctive landscape by soil, vegetation and other clues.

_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

RESOURCE: This image was made possible by the invaluable research done by Jasper Woodard. You can check out his Botswana videos on his YouTube channel.

Coverage in Botswana is fairly limited due to the country’s sparse road system. In addition to regular paved roads, you can still expect to see some rural unpaved road coverage. The most dense coverage is in the east and near Gaborone. The larger towns have extensive side road coverage.
This map shows which covered roads are paved, and which ones are unpaved. It is slightly simplified for ease of reading. Small, unpaved side roads in and near towns are not shown.

Most of Botswana is as flat as a pancake. However, every now and then you will find some elevation. If you see hills, you are most likely in one of the two areas indicated on the minimap.

NOTE: Even in the indicated areas, there are a lot of very flat areas, as many of Botswana’s hills are geographically isolated. Some lone hills may also appear far outside the indicated areas.

The southeastern region near Gaborone has many semi-arid hills covered in short shrubs. If you see a lot of these, you are likely to be in the area between Gaborone and Lobatse.

NOTE: Similar hills can be found elsewhere in the country and across the border in South Africa. If you see a large quantity of them, and use other clues to rule out South Africa, you can be fairly certain that you are in southeastern Botswana.

The landscape in the eastern pocket north of Francistown is characterised by red soil and a somewhat arid look. The soil in these two areas often looks firm and rocky, rather than sandy or dusty. Trees and bushes with yellowed leaves and other “autumn” colours are common. Many trees are bare and withered. You might see fallen leaves on the ground here and there.

A large region in the middle western part of the country is characterised by very white sandy soil. In addition, the vegetation tends to look very dry.

NOTE: Sandy soil can be found in many places in Botswana. This tip specifically refers to the bright white colour of the sand.

The A35 is a very recognisable road: there is always a power line to your west. It can also be recognised by its grainy asphalt with faded markings. Many small tracks can be found parallel to the road, disappearing into the bushes.
The A33 is characterised by a landscape that is more lush than usual. Trees have lots of green leaves and the grass is very tall. The more north you go, the more lush the vegetation becomes.

The road that runs along Botswana’s southern border, through the town of Middlepits, has asphalt with a distinct red tint. The landscape is arid. In some sections, slight hills can be seen.

NOTE: Near the town of Middlepits itself, the soil is very red and dotted with small white pebbles.

Gaborone is the capital and largest city. It tends to look richer and more developed than the rest of Botswana, though some neighbourhoods may still look impoverished. In some southern parts of the city hills can be seen, but most of the town is flat.

NOTE: The only other place in the country that often looks similar is Francistown.

In Francistown, you can often see a lone hill with radio antennas, which is located on the north side of the city. This hill is a good way to distinguish Francistown from Gaborone.

NOTE: The town of Serowe has a similar hill with antennas. Here, the towers are taller, red-and-white striped, and the hill has a flat top.
Maun is the only relatively large city in Botswana that has this bright white sandy soil, which is typical for the middle western region of the country.
The western part of the A2 has overcast coverage, making it recognisable.

Chobe Flood Plains National Park in the far north has a lot of small, winding dirt road coverage, with a lot of it being just south of the Chobe River. It has scattered lush bushes on either side, and you will often find wildlife such as elephants and warthogs.

This portion of the A30 has a distinct autumn feel unique to it. Notably, there are trees with orange coloured leaves lining the road in straight rows. In addition, there is often tall grass as opposed to other autumn looking locations.

Salt pans can be found in central-eastern Botswana. Dirt road coverage can be found leading to the pans and has similar soil and grass, but you can also find many trees along the road. They are mainly found around the Nwetwe pan. The salt pans show up as lakes on the map.

NOTE: A lot of the dirt road coverage near the pans was taken in June, and will feature trees without leaves or those that are beginning to lose their leaves.

Just outside Gaborone, there is a lot of coverage along very rural, small dirt tracks. They can be identified by the orange-red shade of dirt and abundance of green trees and bushes surrounding the road.

The section of the A33 within the Sibuya Forest Reserve and the CT/3 (Tamafupa) Commercial Wildlife Utilisation is under construction. This is most visible by the service road or embankment alongside the road.

NOTE: Despite being in the construction zone, some locations may still look normal.

The mostly unpaved road north of Maun to Khwai can be identified by extremely white sandy soil and tall green trees surrounding the road. The first section of the road, between Maun and Shorobe, is paved. But that section can still be identified by the trees, faint road markings, and power lines to the west of the road.
The A20 has mostly clean, recent asphalt. Some sections of the road are much thinner than usual. The landscape is characterised by red soil, dry grey-coloured trees, and very little grass.

Southeast of Tshabong, the A20 has been recently repainted and has very bright yellow lines and relatively dark asphalt. There is a powerline running alongside it to the northeast, it has orange-tan sandy soil, and you can often find patches of yellow flowers.
The Tsodilo Hills World Heritage Site is memorable due to its large protruding hills with exposed rock faces. The coverage around the hills is entirely on dirt roads.
These distinctive silos are found in Pandamatenga in northeastern Botswana and can be seen all around the town.

lm.name: Chevrons
lm.note:
• These small red-and-white chevrons can sometimes be found next to the road.

--- NOTE:

  • They are also very common in South Africa.

lm.name: - Tsodilo Hills road
lm.note:
The dirt road that runs from the A35 to Tsodilo Hills can be recognized by combining the white sand and the lush vegetation with the road/driving direction (west south-west). It looks a lot like the road north of Maun but that road never goes this direction.

Additionally, the Tsodilo Hills can be seen in most locations in the half of the road closer to the Hills than the A35, since the hills themselves are very tall for Botswana standards. You will also be able to see Venus (wenus) that will be roughly northwest. (I still consider it west venus)

lm.name: A1central - A1 - Central District
lm.note:
The section of the A1 within the Central District (Dibete to Tonota) has a parallel paved road the entire way, which is not in use or painted with road lines. This section is distinguishable from the A1 north of Francistown because it is not newly paved/painted.

The map does not show the parallel road in the south of this section, so remember it stretches across the entire Central District if you are trying to pinpoint.

lm.name: A1north - A1 - North of Francistown
lm.note: The section of the A1 north of Francistown has a road that runs parallel the whole way to the border to its east. It is often a light gray colour. This section of the A1 looks recently paved compared to other parts of the A1 which also have a parallel road.

lm.name: A2west0poles - A2 - West (0 Poles)
lm.note:
West A2 = Most identifiable road in Botswana (the only paved road with overcast coverage)

No electricity poles means you are between the Chobokwane junction and the A2/A3 junction. This coverage also has the sun trying to shine through the clouds instead of complete overcast coverage, but it is still a lot cloudier than almost all Botswana coverage.

lm.name: A2west1pole - A2 - West (1 Pole)
lm.note:
West A2 = Most identifiable road in Botswana (the only paved road with overcast coverage)

One electricity pole means you are between Tshootsha and Chobokwane. The pole should be a shorter pole that stays close and to the north of the road. Make sure a second taller pole is not also visible, even if in the far distance or to the south, as that puts you in the red section instead.

lm.name: A2west2poles - A2 - West (2 Poles)
lm.note:
West A2 = Most identifiable road in Botswana (the only paved road with overcast coverage)

Two electricity poles means you are between Charleshill and Tshootsha. The first pole should be a shorter one thats stays close and to the north of the road. The second pole is a taller one and can be in any direction and distance relative to you, north or south. However, it will always be visible, just make sure you check thoroughly if you can't initially see it. Finally, use the road angle to know if you are east or west of Karakubis.

lm.name: A32 - A32
lm.note: The A32 is an identifiable road located west of the main salt pans in central Botswana. The most noticeable thing is the red/grey tint to the dead-looking trees either side of the road. Combine this with the white dirt on the sides of the road to know you are here.

lm.name: A33construction - A33 - Road Construction
lm.note: A significant portion of the A33 has a road under construction next to it. This road can have dug up orange soil, white soil, be somewhat paved, or just have the long grass cut. Regardless, when combined with the relatively green trees, you will almost certainly be on this section of road.

lm.name: A33farmland - A33 - Crop Fields
lm.note: The highlighted locations are basically the only sections of road in the entire country where large fields of small crop plants are visible in rows like these. Use the road angle to know which of the two sections you are in.

lm.name: A33newroad - A33 - Newly Paved Section
lm.note: A significant portion of the A33 is made up of a newly paved road. This road is very wide, has no roadlines yet, and both sides of the road have almost been completely dug up. No other section of road in Botswana looks quite like this.

lm.name: A33south - A33 - South Section
lm.note:
This section of the A33 is distinguishable by combining the good-quality road with either the colourful trees or the tall golden grass that has a shine to it from distance.

Nearby areas can have similar coverage, but this road looks recently paved/painted and no other road with similar coverage is as vertical on the map as this section is. You will also see an electricity pole on this section of road between Nata and Maposa.

lm.name: A35bothpoles - A35 - East + West Poles
lm.note:
The road quality of the A35 is relatively bad with the side paving being uneven, and the faded yellow line is usually on this part of the road. There is also a lot of yellow grass, with yellow and green shrubs and trees.

Only a small section in the centre of the A35 has an electricity pole both east and west (excluding in villages, which looks different). Additionally, an even smaller section has the west electricity lines seemingly broken, and the lines can either be seen running in trees or on the ground.

lm.name: A35eastpole - A35 - East Pole
lm.note:
The road quality of the A35 is relatively bad with the side paving being uneven, and the faded yellow line is usually on this part of the road. There is also a lot of yellow grass, with yellow and green shrubs and trees.

You will only find an electricity pole to the east of the road below Tsau, which makes for an amazing region guess.

lm.name: A35village - A35 - Villages
lm.note:
The road quality of the A35 is relatively bad with the side paving being uneven, and the faded yellow line is usually on this part of the road. There is also a lot of yellow grass, with yellow and green shrubs and trees.

Small villages run up the entire A35. If you see electricity poles which go across the road, where there are multiple lines on one side of the road, or rare coverage where none are visible, you will be in/near a village.

lm.name: A35westpole - A35 - West Pole
lm.note:
The road quality of the A35 is relatively bad with the side paving being uneven, and the faded yellow line is usually on this part of the road. There is also a lot of yellow grass, with yellow and green shrubs and trees.

Unfortunately a majority of the A35 has an electricity pole to the west of the road. It does at least put you north of Tsau and rule out a small section in the middle.

lm.name: A3east - A3 - Nata to Francistown
lm.note: This eastern part of the A3 is identifiable by the colourful trees on the sides of the road. To tell this apart from other similar coverage, look at the road. This area is not recently paved, and the grass is basically touching the yellow road lines.

lm.name: backleft blur - backleft blur
lm.note: the part on the a14 is iffy of whether or not it is the back left blur. It is most useful for the Road in the North. the blur is square/rectangle in shape.

lm.name: black thing - black thing
lm.note: look up and its there

lm.name: border SA - South West - Border with South Africa
lm.note:
The furthest south-west road in Botswana runs along the border with South Africa. You can tell you are here by the redness of the road and surrounding sand/dirt and the pale-green grass which is visible a lot of the time. Additionally, there is almost always a slight hill to the north (sometimes south too).

One important thing to note is the car drives the road from east to west (of course accounting for the road's bends). This can help rule out certain spots of road that wouldn't make logical sense if you want to try and 5k.

lm.name: Area Code - Francistown
lm.note:
All helpful numbers in Botswana will be 7 digits long, not 8.

If you find a 7 digit number that is 24X XXXX, it is based in Francistown.

lm.name: charlesnco - West - Charleshill to Ncojane
lm.note: The road furthest west in Botswana is easy to identify. It looks the same as most of the other unpaved roads found in the west of the country, but this road is identifiable from the electricity pole to the east of the road. This does not diverge from the road once.

lm.name: choberiver - North Border - Chobe River
lm.note: The Chobe River, which makes up part of Botswana's northern border, is rarely seen but easy to recognize. It can have patches of tall grass peeking out the top of the water and a variety of wildlife can often be seen in the area, including elephants, warthogs, and much more. If you can see the wide river, you will almost certainly be on one of the paths in a circled zone.

lm.name: code3 - Area Code - Gaborone
lm.note:
All helpful numbers in Botswana will be 7 digits long, not 8.

If you find a 7 digit number that is 3XX XXXX, it is based in Gaborone. However, many companies that provide services outside Gaborone are still based in the capital which can make this area code a little less reliable. Try to find a number on a building rather than a vehicle or advertising sign if possible.

lm.name: code68 - Area Code - Maun
lm.note:
All helpful numbers in Botswana will be 7 digits long, not 8.

If you find a 7 digit number that is 68X XXXX, it is based in Maun.

lm.name: Diamond/ - Diamond Reflectors
lm.note: This is the only road in Botswana that has the reflectors laid out in a diamond shape. Usually, all 3 are in a line spanning the width of the road, but here the outside are still adjacent to each other but the middle is not, forming a diamond with the next set of reflectors.

lm.name: East A30 - East A30
lm.note: The Eastern section of the A30 is very easily confused with A3 east of Maun because the vegatation, road color, and road angle are extremely similar. One Key defference is that the A3 has eoon (east moon) while this road does not.

lm.name: eenus - eenus
lm.note: east venus

lm.name: eoon - eoon
lm.note: east moon

lm.name: fog - fog
lm.note: “Fog” coverage is characterized with big suns and way more grey than blue skies. Looking away from the sun in this image, but seeing almost no blue.

lm.name: front smudge - front smudge
lm.note: Frontal Smudge Only Found on these roads

lm.name: latvian poles - latvian poles
lm.note: this cooler looking latvian poletop can only be found on this stretch of the a30, west of orapa up to mopipi. its actually pretty common in the stretch of powerlines south

lm.name: maununpaved - North Maun - Unpaved Road
lm.note: One of the most recognizable unpaved roads in Botswana is north of Maun. Starting in Shorobe, this road has white sand and bright green trees the entire way. Try to use the road angle and road width to your advantage too, for example the central coverage has a lot of curves in the road and goes north-west.

lm.name: Misaligned/L - Misaligned Reflectors
lm.note: The reflectors on this section of road were misplaced. They are not perfectly in the middle of the dashes and are offcenterd. The dashes on this road are Long dashes (as opposed to short dashes)

lm.name: nenus - nenus
lm.note: north venus

lm.name: No bushes - No Bushes
lm.note: This section of road has no bushes or anything, it is just a large salt pan.

lm.name: nonpavedwest - West - Non-Paved Roads
lm.note: All the highlighted roads look similar with white sand for the road and surrounded by either orange sand or yellow grass. They are also unpaved and have no electricity poles. If you think you are here, try to remember the google car directions to know where would be best to guess.

lm.name: noon - noon
lm.note: north moon

lm.name: senus - senus
lm.note: south venus

lm.name: shitback - shitback
lm.note: stuff on car

lm.name: Short/4 - Short Dashes (4)
lm.note:
These sections of roads have Short Dashes with Reflectors spaced every 4 dashes.

There are two types of dashes in Botswana - Long and Short. Click around on paved roads to get a feel for which is which.

lm.name: shoshong - Shoshong Hills
lm.note: The town of Shoshong and the surrounding roads are identifiable. There is a long stretch of tall hills to the north and south and it generally looks like the hills completely surround the area. The few other places in Botswana where hills surround the area have much closer hills, but the ones around Shoshong are visible even from far away.

lm.name: sticker - sticker
lm.note: not always visible

lm.name: threads - threads
lm.note: different every pano.

lm.name: top smudge - top smudge
lm.note: This top Smudge can be seen on these roads. Most useful for the ones in the south

lm.name: wenus - wenus
lm.note: west venus

lm.name: white grainy pavement - White Grainy Pavement
lm.note: White Grainy Pavement- The road itself is more white than anything else, and is very grainy.

lm.name: woon - woon
lm.note: west moon

lm.name: Shacks & Bungalows
lm.note:
• Typical Botswana houses range from small impoverished shacks to comfortable middle-class bungalows.
  • Some buildings have exposed grey bricks.
  • On occasion, you might find traditional round huts.

--- NOTE:

  • All of these house styles are also found in the other southern African countries.

lm.name: A20
lm.note: The A20 has mostly clean, recent asphalt. Some sections of the road are much thinner than usual. The landscape is characterised by red soil, dry grey-coloured trees, and very little grass

lm.name: A20 - southeast of Tshabong
lm.note: Southeast of Tshabong, the A20 has been recently repainted and has very bright yellow lines and relatively dark asphalt. There is a powerline running alongside it to the northeast, it has orange-tan sandy soil, and you can often find patches of yellow flowers.

lm.note: These distinctive silos are found in Pandamatenga in northeastern Botswana and can be seen all around the town.

lm.note: Just outside Gaborone, there is a lot of coverage along very rural, small dirt tracks. They can be identified by the orange-red shade of dirt and abundance of green trees and bushes surrounding the road.

Salt pans can be found in central-eastern Botswana. Dirt road coverage can be found leading to the pans and has similar soil and grass, but you can also find many trees along the road. They are mainly found around the Nwetwe pan. The salt pans show up as lakes on the map.

The section of the A33 within the Sibuya Forest Reserve and the CT/3 (Tamafupa) Commercial Wildlife Utilisation is under construction. This is most visible by the service road or embankment alongside the road.

NOTE: Despite being in the construction zone, some locations may still look normal.

lm.note: The Tsodilo Hills World Heritage Site is memorable due to its large protruding hills with exposed rock faces. The coverage around the hills is entirely on dirt roads.

lm.name: Western part of the A2
lm.note: The western part of the A2 has overcast coverage, making it recognisable.

lm.name: A33 Lush Landscape
lm.note:
• The A33 is characterised by a landscape that is more lush than usual.
  • Trees have lots of green leaves and the grass is very tall.
  • The more north you go, the more lush the vegetation becomes.

lm.name: A35 Power Line
lm.note:
The A35 is a very recognisable road:

  • There is always a power line to your west.
  • It can also be recognised by its grainy asphalt with faded markings.
  • Many small tracks can be found parallel to the road, disappearing into the bushes.

lm.name: Francistown Antennas
lm.note:
• In Francistown, you can often see a lone hill with radio antennas, which is located on the north side of the city.
  • This hill is a good way to distinguish Francistown from Gaborone.

NOTE:

  • The town of Serowe has a similar hill with antennas.
  • Here, the towers are taller, red-and-white striped, and the hill has a flat top.

lm.name: Gaborone
lm.note:
• Gaborone is the capital and largest city.
  • It tends to look richer and more developed than the rest of Botswana, though some neighbourhoods may still look impoverished.
  • In some southern parts of the city hills can be seen, but most of the town is flat.

NOTE:

  • The only other place in the country that often looks similar is Francistown.

lm.name: Hills
lm.note:
• Most of Botswana is as flat as a pancake.
  • If you see hills, you are most likely in one of the two areas indicated on the minimap.

NOTE:

  • Even in the indicated areas, there are a lot of very flat areas, as many of Botswana’s hills are geographically isolated.
  • Some lone hills may also appear far outside the indicated areas.

lm.name: Maun Bright Sand
lm.note: • Maun is the only relatively large city in Botswana that has this bright white sandy soil, which is typical for the middle western region of the country.

lm.name: Red Road
lm.note:
• The road that runs along Botswana’s southern border, through the town of Middlepits, has asphalt with a distinct red tint.
  • The landscape is arid.
  • In some sections, slight hills can be seen.

NOTE:

  • Near the town of Middlepits itself, the soil is very red and dotted with small white pebbles.

lm.name: Red Soil
lm.note:
• The landscape in the eastern pocket north of Francistown is characterised by red soil and a somewhat arid look.
  • The soil in these two areas often looks firm and rocky, rather than sandy or dusty.
  • Trees and bushes with yellowed leaves and other “autumn” colours are common.

lm.name: Semi Arid Hills
lm.note:
• The southeastern region near Gaborone has many semi-arid hills covered in short shrubs.
  • If you see a lot of these, you are likely to be in the area between Gaborone and Lobatse.

NOTE:

  • Similar hills can be found elsewhere in the country and across the border in South Africa.
  • If you see a large quantity of them, and use other clues to rule out South Africa, you can be fairly certain that you are in southeastern Botswana.

lm.name: White Sandy Soil
lm.note:
• A large region in the middle western part of the country is characterised by very white sandy soil.
  • In addition, the vegetation tends to look very dry.

NOTE:

  • Sandy soil can be found in many places in Botswana.
  • This tip specifically refers to the bright white colour of the sand.

lm.name: A1 - Central District
lm.note:
The section of the A1 within the Central District (Dibete to Tonota) has a parallel paved road the entire way, which is not in use or painted with road lines. Parallel roads are basically only found on the A1, and this section is distinguishable from the A1 north of Francistown because it is not newly paved/painted.

The map does not show the parallel road in the south of this section, so remember it stretches across the entire Central District if you are trying to pinpoint.

lm.name: A1 - North of Francistown
lm.note: The section of the A1 north of Francistown has a road that runs parallel the whole way to the border to its east. It is often a light gray colour. This section of the A1 looks recently paved compared to other parts of the A1 which also have a parallel road.

lm.name: A2 - West (0 Poles)
lm.note:
West A2 = Most identifiable road in Botswana (the only paved road with overcast coverage)

No electricity poles means you are between the Chobokwane junction and the A2/A3 junction. This coverage also has the sun trying to shine through the clouds instead of complete overcast coverage, but it is still a lot cloudier than almost all Botswana coverage.

lm.name: A2 - West (1 Pole)
lm.note:
West A2 = Most identifiable road in Botswana (the only paved road with overcast coverage)

One electricity pole means you are between Tshootsha and Chobokwane. The pole should be a shorter pole that stays close and to the north of the road. Make sure a second taller pole is not also visible, even if in the far distance or to the south, as that puts you in the red section instead.

lm.name: A2 - West (2 Poles)
lm.note:
West A2 = Most identifiable road in Botswana (the only paved road with overcast coverage)

Two electricity poles means you are between Charleshill and Tshootsha. The first pole should be a shorter one thats stays close and to the north of the road. The second pole is a taller one and can be in any direction and distance relative to you, north or south. However, it will always be visible, just make sure you check thoroughly if you can't initially see it. Finally, use the road angle to know if you are east or west of Karakubis.

lm.name: A3 - Nata to Francistown
lm.note: This eastern part of the A3 is identifiable by the colourful trees on the sides of the road. To tell this apart from other similar coverage, look at the road. This area is not recently paved, and the grass is basically touching the yellow road lines.

lm.name: A32
lm.note: The A32 is an identifiable road located west of the main salt pans in central Botswana. The most noticeable thing is the red/grey tint to the dead-looking trees either side of the road. Combine this with the white dirt on the sides of the road to know you are here.

lm.name: A33 - Crop Fields
lm.note: The highlighted locations are basically the only sections of road in the entire country where large fields of small crop plants are visible in rows like these. Use the road angle to know which of the two sections you are in.

lm.name: A33 - Newly Paved Section
lm.note: A significant portion of the A33 is made up of a newly paved road. This road is very wide, has no roadlines yet, and both sides of the road have almost been completely dug up. No other section of road in Botswana looks quite like this.

lm.name: A33 - Road Construction
lm.note: A significant portion of the A33 has a road under construction next to it. This road can have dug up orange soil, white soil, be somewhat paved, or just have the long grass cut. Regardless, when combined with the relatively green trees, you will almost certainly be on this section of road.

lm.name: A33 - South Section
lm.note:
This section of the A33 is distinguishable by combining the good-quality road with either the colourful trees or the tall golden grass that has a shine to it from distance.

Nearby areas can have similar coverage, but this road looks recently paved/painted and no other road with similar coverage is as vertical on the map as this section is. You will also see an electricity pole on this section of road between Nata and Maposa.

lm.name: A35 - East + West Poles
lm.note:
The road quality of the A35 is relatively bad with the side paving being uneven, and the faded yellow line is usually on this part of the road. There is also a lot of yellow grass, with yellow and green shrubs and trees.

Only a small section in the centre of the A35 has an electricity pole both east and west (excluding in villages, which looks different). Additionally, an even smaller section has the west electricity lines seemingly broken, and the lines can either be seen running in trees or on the ground.

lm.name: A35 - East Pole
lm.note:
The road quality of the A35 is relatively bad with the side paving being uneven, and the faded yellow line is usually on this part of the road. There is also a lot of yellow grass, with yellow and green shrubs and trees.

You will only find an electricity pole to the east of the road below Tsau, which makes for an amazing region guess.

lm.name: A35 - Villages
lm.note:
The road quality of the A35 is relatively bad with the side paving being uneven, and the faded yellow line is usually on this part of the road. There is also a lot of yellow grass, with yellow and green shrubs and trees.

Small villages run up the entire A35. If you see electricity poles which go across the road, where there are multiple lines on one side of the road, or rare coverage where none are visible, you will be in/near a village.

lm.name: A35 - West Pole
lm.note:
The road quality of the A35 is relatively bad with the side paving being uneven, and the faded yellow line is usually on this part of the road. There is also a lot of yellow grass, with yellow and green shrubs and trees.

Unfortunately a majority of the A35 has an electricity pole to the west of the road. It does at least put you north of Tsau and rule out a small section in the middle.

lm.name: Area Code - Francistown
lm.note:
All helpful numbers in Botswana will be 7 digits long, not 8.

If you find a 7 digit number that is 24X XXXX, it is based in Francistown.

lm.name: Area Code - Gaborone
lm.note:
All helpful numbers in Botswana will be 7 digits long, not 8.

If you find a 7 digit number that is 3XX XXXX, it is based in Gaborone. However, many companies that provide services outside Gaborone are still based in the capital which can make this area code a little less reliable. Try to find a number on a building rather than a vehicle or advertising sign if possible.

lm.name: Area Code - Maun
lm.note:
All helpful numbers in Botswana will be 7 digits long, not 8.

If you find a 7 digit number that is 68X XXXX, it is based in Maun.

lm.name: North Border - Chobe River
lm.note: The Chobe River, which makes up part of Botswana's northern border, is rarely seen but easy to recognize. It can have patches of tall grass peeking out the top of the water and a variety of wildlife can often be seen in the area, including elephants, warthogs, and much more. If you can see the wide river, you will almost certainly be on one of the paths in a circled zone.

lm.name: North Maun - Unpaved Road
lm.note: One of the most recognizable unpaved roads in Botswana is north of Maun. Starting in Shorobe, this road has white sand and bright green trees the entire way. Try to use the road angle and road width to your advantage too, for example the central coverage has a lot of curves in the road and goes north-west.

lm.name: Shoshong Hills
lm.note: The town of Shoshong and the surrounding roads are identifiable. There is a long stretch of tall hills to the north and south and it generally looks like the hills completely surround the area. The few other places in Botswana where hills surround the area have much closer hills, but the ones around Shoshong are visible even from far away.

lm.name: South West - Border with South Africa
lm.note:
The furthest south-west road in Botswana runs along the border with South Africa. You can tell you are here by the redness of the road and surrounding sand/dirt and the pale-green grass which is visible a lot of the time. Additionally, there is almost always a slight hill to the north (sometimes south too).

One important thing to note is the car drives the road from east to west (of course accounting for the road's bends). This can help rule out certain spots of road that wouldn't make logical sense if you want to try and 5k.

lm.name: Tsodilo Hills Road
lm.note:
Tsodilo Hills is a world heritage site in north-west Botswana branching off the A35. The single dirt road that runs from the A35 to Tsodilo Hills can be recognized by combining the white sand and the lush vegetation with the road/driving direction (west south-west). It looks a lot like the road north of Maun but that road never goes this direction.

Additionally, the Tsodilo Hills can be seen in most locations in the half of the road closer to the Hills than the A35, since the hills themselves are very tall for Botswana standards.

lm.name: West - Charleshill to Ncojane
lm.note: The road furthest west in Botswana is easy to identify. It looks the same as most of the other unpaved roads found in the west of the country, but this road is identifiable from the electricity pole to the east of the road. This does not diverge from the road once.

lm.name: West - Non-Paved Roads
lm.note: All the highlighted roads look similar with white sand for the road and surrounded by either orange sand or yellow grass. They are also unpaved and have no electricity poles. If you think you are here, try to remember the google car directions to know where would be best to guess.

lm.name: Vibes
lm.note:
A dry, flat landscape with African vegetation, usually a bit away from the road, is a good clue for Botswana and becomes quite distinct after seeing it couple times. You can confirm it's Botswana by the white back of the Google car, driving on the left, yellow outer lines, and the sun in the north.

The only other countries in Africa with that combination are:

  • Eswatini & Lesotho (but they will be hilly)
  • South Africa (though this is rare, as most of the coverage now is with blue back of the google car).

lm.name: Roadlines
lm.note:
• Like the other countries in Southern Africa, outside road lines (if present) are yellow, while centre road lines are white.

--- NOTE:

  • Outside yellow road lines in arid environments also exist in Israel, Palestine, Jordan, and the UAE.
  • However, these countries all drive on the right side.

lm.name: pole
lm.note:
In Botswana, most poles are generic wooden poles with a wooden top.

NOTE: South Africa also use this type of pole

top.html:
All of Botswana was covered by a white Google car without an antenna.

NOTE: Within Africa, this car can also be found in South Africa, Lesotho and Eswatini.
top.raw: All of Botswana was covered by a **white** Google car without an antenna. NOTE: Within Africa, this car can also be found in South Africa, Lesotho and Eswatini.

top.html:
Botswana has white front plates and yellow rear plates, similar to UK-style plates.

NOTE: Botswana and Namibia are the only countries in southern Africa where yellow rear plates are predominantly found.
top.raw: Botswana has **white** front plates and **yellow** rear plates, similar to UK-style plates. NOTE: Botswana and Namibia are the only countries in southern Africa where yellow rear plates are predominantly found.

top.html:
Signs in Botswana are usually in English. Most town names, however, are derived from any of the indigenous languages spoken in the country.

NOTE: The Afrikaans language, which is closely related to Dutch and common in South Africa, is very rare in Botswana. You will almost never find Afrikaans place names.

NOTE: The Afrikaans language, which is closely related to Dutch and common in South Africa, is very rare in Botswana. You will almost never find Afrikaans place names.

top.html:
The typical Botswana landscape is dry and mostly flat, though a limited amount of elevation can be found in certain regions. Common vegetation includes shrubs, small trees, and occasionally dry, golden grasslands. The soil is arid, sandy and ranges in colour from white to red.

NOTE: The border region of South Africa can have a similar landscape.

Common vegetation includes shrubs, small trees, and occasionally dry, golden grasslands. The soil is arid, sandy and ranges in colour from white to red. NOTE: The border region of South Africa can have a similar landscape.

top.html:
Like the other countries in Southern Africa, outside road lines (if present) are yellow, while centre road lines are white.

NOTE: Outside yellow road lines in arid environments also exist in Israel, Palestine, Jordan, and the UAE. However, these countries all drive on the right side.

NOTE: Outside yellow road lines in arid environments also exist in Israel, Palestine, Jordan, and the UAE. However, these countries all drive on the right side.

top.html:
Botswana has a unique black-and-yellow striped signpost. More rarely, you can see red-and-white signposts.

NOTE: In Southern Africa, these signposts are only found in Botswana.
top.raw: Botswana has a unique **black-and-yellow striped signpost**. More rarely, you can see red-and-white signposts. NOTE: In Southern Africa, these signposts are only found in Botswana.

top.html: Curbs and guardrails are usually striped. Possible colour schemes are black-and-yellow, red-and-white, and black-and-white.
top.raw: Curbs and guardrails are usually **striped**. Possible colour schemes are black-and-yellow, red-and-white, and black-and-white.

top.html:
These small red-and-white chevrons can sometimes be found next to the road.

NOTE: They are also very common in South Africa.
top.raw: These small **red-and-white chevrons** can sometimes be found next to the road. NOTE: They are also very common in South Africa.

top.html:
Just like the other Southern African countries, direction signs have a green background.

The numbers of major roads start with A. These road numbers frequently appear on direction signs.

NOTE: Road numbers in South Africa never start with A.
top.raw: Just like the other Southern African countries, direction signs have a **green background**. The numbers of major roads start with **A**. These road numbers frequently appear on direction signs. NOTE: Road numbers in South Africa never start with A.

top.html:
Some road signs have a blue background. This is an older style of sign that was used before signs with white backgrounds were introduced. They are relatively unique to Botswana.

Note that most road signs will have the newer white background.
top.raw: Some road signs have a **blue background**. This is an older style of sign that was used before signs with white backgrounds were introduced. They are relatively unique to Botswana. Note that most road signs will have the newer white background.

top.html:
Typical Botswana houses range from small impoverished shacks to comfortable middle-class bungalows. Some buildings have exposed grey bricks. On occasion, you might find traditional round huts.

NOTE: All of these house styles are also found in the other southern African countries.

top.html: Random small blurs are common in Botswana’s coverage. These blurs are similar to the ones found on licence plates and faces, but they cover seemingly random parts of the panorama instead. This is especially noticeable in urban areas, and mostly absent on more rural roads.
